claim: Raft's Section 2 defines replicated state machines as state machines on a collection of servers that compute identical copies of the same state and keep operating even when some servers are down.
quote: Consensus algorithms typically arise in the context of replicated state machines. In this approach, state machines on a collection of servers compute identical copies of the same state and can continue operating even if some of the servers are down.

locator: Section 2 'Replicated state machines', p.2 (the example paragraph)
claim: Section 2's opening example is large-scale systems with a single cluster leader (GFS, HDFS, RAMCloud) that use a separate replicated state machine to manage leader election and store configuration that must survive leader crashes, citing Chubby and ZooKeeper.
quote: For example, large-scale systems that have a single cluster leader, such as GFS [8], HDFS [38], and RAMCloud [33], typically use a separate replicated state machine to manage leader election and store configuration information that must survive leader crashes. Examples of replicated state machines include Chubby [2] and ZooKeeper [11].

claim: The consensus module on a server accepts commands from clients into its log and communicates with the other servers' consensus modules so that every log eventually holds the same requests in the same order, even if some servers fail.
quote: The consensus module on a server receives commands from clients and adds them to its log. It communicates with the consensus modules on other servers to ensure that every log eventually contains the same requests in the same order, even if some servers fail.

claim: For understandability, Raft separates consensus into the key elements leader election, log replication, and safety, and reduces the number of states to consider.
quote: In order to enhance understandability, Raft separates the key elements of consensus, such as leader election, log replication, and safety, and it enforces a stronger degree of coherency to reduce the number of states that must be considered.

claim: Lamport's three safety requirements are: only a proposed value may be chosen, only a single value is chosen, and a process never learns a value was chosen unless it actually was.
quote: The safety requirements for consensus are: Only a value that has been proposed may be chosen, Only a single value is chosen, and A process never learns that a value has been chosen unless it actually has been.

claim: When two proposers each complete phase 1 with successively increasing proposal numbers, the lower-numbered proposer's phase-2 accept requests are ignored because the acceptors promised not to accept anything numbered below the higher number, so neither proposal is chosen.
quote: Proposer p completes phase 1 for a proposal number n1. Another proposer q then completes phase 1 for a proposal number n2 > n1. Proposer p's phase 2 accept requests for a proposal numbered n1 are ignored because the acceptors have all promised not to accept any new proposal numbered less than n2.

claim: The fix for the dueling-proposer livelock is to guarantee progress by selecting a distinguished proposer as the only one that tries to issue proposals.
quote: To guarantee progress, a distinguished proposer must be selected as the only one to try issuing proposals.
